title: Enforcement signal propagation and region segmentation notes
body:
Context and goal:

Short: capture pragmatic enforcement placement for routing/control-plane across regions with an eye toward latency, correctness, and rollout safety. These are working notes — wants and constraints, plus sketch proposals for prototypes.

Why this matters now:
- Dedicated + Private customers want strict isolation and audit trails; hosted needs predictable SLOs.
- We need clear guidance for where authz decisions are evaluated (edge, regional router, model-proxy, central PDP) and how signals move between layers without exploding per-request latency.

Main constraints we care about:
- Latency SLO: control-plane decision path should add <12ms p50 if possible; data-plane per-request authz should not exceed 30ms p95 for hosted API use-cases.
- Correctness: no request that violates policy should be routed to restricted model or tenant.
- Survivability: regions can be partitioned — we must pick safe defaults for stale policy TTLs and fail-open vs fail-closed behavior per zone and customer profile.
- Operational simplicity: policy rollouts, canaries, and immediate revocation use cases (e.g., compromised API key).

Key concepts / vocabulary (working):
- enforcement hop: a network/compute boundary that can apply a decision (edge-proxy, regional-router, model-proxy, control-plane PDP).
- carried-claims: signed, short-lived metadata added to request headers by an upstream enforcement hop (e.g., signed-claims: base64(jwt-like)) that downstream hops can trust without re-evaluating full policy.
- local PDP: lightweight evaluator co-located with a hop that can evaluate a subset of policies (ABAC predicates cached) quickly.
- central PDP: authoritative policy engine in control-plane; used for management, audit, and as fallback.
- policy fingerprint: monotonic, compact ID for a given policy state/version to detect staleness and invalidation.

Deployment pattern options (pro/con):
1) Edge-first (push decisions to the edge):
   - Pros: minimal cross-region calls, lower tail latency, decisions close to request source.
   - Cons: policy distribution/consistency challenge, larger attack surface for policy bugs, complexity in revocation.

2) Regional PDP with signed claims propagation:
   - Pros: balances latency and control; regional PDPs evaluate and emit carried-claims; downstream model-proxies only verify signature + TTL.
   - Cons: needs secure signing keys per-region + key rotation and centralized revocation list.

3) Central PDP with optimistic caching at hops:
   - Pros: single source of truth, easier audit, easier immediate revocation by central decisions.
   - Cons: higher cross-region latency; needs robust caching layer with invalidation; can create availability coupling.

Recommended hybrid (prototype): regional PDP + carried-claims + central audit/override
- Regional PDPs evaluate most requests (ABAC, RBAC mapping) and sign a carried-claims header containing: requester.id, requester.roles, resource.labels, decision.ttl, policy-fingerprint, request-id.
- Downstream enforcement hops (model-proxy, file-store-router) verify signature and TTL and perform lightweight checks. If carried-claims missing or expired, hop falls back to local PDP if available, otherwise calls regional PDP synchronously (with circuit-breaker).
- Central PDP maintains authoritative policy and publishes policy fingerprints & signed key material via secure config distribution (mTLS + versioned bundles).

Attributes to include in ABAC evaluation (suggested set):
- requester.id, requester.team, requester.trust_level
- caller_origin (region, ip_range), connection_type (internal/edge)
- resource.type, resource.sensitivity (P0,P1,P2), resource.tenant_id
- operation (transform, generate, embed, admin-config)
- model.metadata (name, quantization_profile, version, signed_runtime_fingerprint)
- time-of-day (for maintenance windows), active_incident_flag

RBAC mapping notes:
- Keep RBAC stable and coarse-grained: roles map to permission sets; ABAC predicates handle edge cases and dynamic constraints.
- Role membership may be resolved by a separate service (identity->roles); cache role sets at regional PDP with TTL tied to user session or token revocation stream.

Caching and invalidation strategy (practical):
- Use policy fingerprints with TTLs. Each carried-claims carries policy-fingerprint_{id}@{version}. Hops compare inlined fingerprint to their local bundle. If mismatch, either revalidate or flag for enforcement downgrade.
- Fast revoke: central service publishes a signed revocation list via streaming (Kafka/replicated etcd) and also a short-lived push mechanism for high-priority revocations (sensitive key compromise).
- Cache TTL heuristics: default 60s for user-scoped decisions; 300s for tenant-level role maps; allow lower TTLs for Dedicated/Private customers who request stronger revocation guarantees.

Signature & key management:
- Regions hold ephemeral signing keys rotated frequently (default 12h). Central KMS holds root keys and signs region keys.
- Verification is symmetric: hops only need public key with short validity window; rotation done via signed key bundles.
- Consider HSM-backed signing for high-tier customers.

Fallback and safety modes:
- fail-closed: for high-sensitivity flows (admin actions, billing changes) prefer fail-closed on any uncertainty.
- fail-open with degraded policy: for low-risk inference traffic we may accept stale carried-claims if signed and TTL within extended window, but record audit and set toll metrics.
- isolation mode: for Private deployments, default to fail-closed by policy and require local PDP availability.

Operational flows (rollouts / canary):
- Policy changes produce a new policy bundle + fingerprint. Publish to central then to regions in phased rollout: canary region -> 10% traffic -> all regions.
- During canary, regional PDP should record divergence metrics: decision-diff-counts between local and central PDP for a set of replayed requests. Use these to detect unintended denials/permits.
- Emergency revoke: central publishes revocation and a forced increment of fingerprint that causes downstream request verification mismatches and forces re-eval against central PDP.

Testing checklist (for any enforcement prototype):
- fuzz policies against representative traffic (generate synthetic ABAC attributes)
- simulate region partition with different policy versions and validate safety properties (no unauthorized access allowed if central says deny)
- load-test cache-hit vs miss paths to identify tail latency hotspots
- audit logs: ensure every decision includes policy-fingerprint, evaluator-id (region), and request-id for traceability

Open questions / TODOs:
- TTL defaults per customer tier: recommended values above are a starting point but need product guidance (GTM/CS input).
- Signature format: compact JWT or binary mac? Evaluate perf on p95 for model-proxy in Rust vs Go.
- How much policy logic should live in model-proxy? Only allow attribute checks and policy fingerprint mismatch handling, not complex joins.
- Key compromise playbook: automated rollback vs manual — document scenarios.

Immediate next steps (proposed short-term roadmap):
1) Prototype regional PDP + carried-claims in staging for one simple policy class (tenant isolation for multi-tenant models). INF-2345 assigned.
2) Build a small verifier library (Go + Rust) used by model-proxy and edge-proxy to verify carried-claims signature and TTL.
3) Add instrumentation: decision source tag, fingerprint mismatch counter, fallback-to-central counter.
4) Run canary using synthetic traffic and record decision diff with central PDP replay for 48h before wider rollout.

Appendix (notes to self):
- Keep enforcement hop list short and opinionated: edge (ingress+authn), regional-pdp (authority), model-proxy (light verify + enforcement), control-plane (audit + override).
- For Private deployments, prefer local PDP + external sync and decrease TTLs to near-zero for critical operations.
- Capture common failure modes in runbook: expired claims spike after rotation, key sync lag, central PDP throttled during incident.

References and tickets:
- INF-2345: regional-pdp prototype
- Confluence: Authz Patterns (linked above)
- GH: plat-authz verifier lib (linked above)

Notes: these are intentionally pragmatic / incremental rather than grand architecture. Aim to prototype quickly and validate safety/latency tradeoffs with real traffic traces.

-- Aisha
